fix(streams): removing a read filter threw away the bytes it had already produced

A read filter reads its whole input to produce a few bytes, so removing it mid-read leaves a
remainder on the stream. php serves that remainder. elephc lost it:

    fread($h, 3)            php "ABC"  ftell 3  feof false     elephc same
    stream_filter_remove()  php true   ftell 3  feof false     elephc ftell 6, feof TRUE
    fread($h, 3)            php "DEF"  ftell 6  feof false     elephc ""
    fread($h, 3)            php ""              feof true      elephc same

On a 10 000-byte file php recovers every byte; elephc recovered 1 818. Silently — the reads
succeed, they just stop early.

THREE helpers had the same defect, and it is the same sentence in each: they asked "is a filter
chain ATTACHED?" where the question is "did this stream go through the filtered buffer?".
`stream_filter_remove()` answers the first no while leaving the second yes, so `__rt_fread`,
`__rt_stream_filtered_pos` and `__rt_stream_eof_get` all jumped to the descriptor — which the
filter had driven far ahead of anything the reader had seen. The bytes were still sitting in the
stream's own buffer, unreachable.

The guard is now the buffer pointer in all three. `__rt_stream_filtered_pos` already tested it as
its SECOND condition, so there the chain test simply goes.

`feof()` needed one more thing, and php's rule is what decides it: `feof()` is never about where
the descriptor is, it is about whether a read ATTEMPT came back empty. The filtered buffer already
models that with its flushed flag — "the filter can emit nothing more" — so the drained no-chain
route sets it on the way to the raw path. Once the filter is gone and its buffer is empty, nothing
more can come from it, which is exactly what that flag asserts. The four-step sequence above then
reproduces php's, step for step.

A LIB TEST PINNED THE OLD RULE and had to move with it. It asserted both guards and gave each a
reason; the chain half's reason — "an unfiltered stream would report a field nothing ever writes"
— is already covered by the buffer-pointer half, since a stream that never engaged the buffered
path has a null buffer pointer. So the guard was redundant for what it claimed and wrong for what
it did. The test now refuses the chain test coming BACK, and still pins the buffer half, whose
reason is real: a filtered stream read only through `fgets()` never touches that buffer and must
fall through to the descriptor probe.
EOF
